content: Hematology, also spelled haematology in British English, is a specialized branch of biology and medicine that focuses on the study of blood, the organs responsible for blood production, and blood-related diseases. It encompasses various disciplines, including physiology, pathology, clinical laboratory science, internal medicine, and pediatrics. Hematology involves the investigation of the causes (etiology), diagnosis, treatment, prognosis, and prevention of blood disorders. Laboratory work related to the study of blood is typically conducted by medical technologists. Blood diseases can affect the production and function of blood and its components, such as blood cells, hemoglobin, blood proteins, and the coagulation process. Physicians who specialize in hematology are referred to as hematologists. Their primary responsibilities include the care and treatment of patients with hematological disorders. Some hematologists also work in hematology laboratories, where they examine blood films and bone marrow slides under a microscope and interpret various hematological test results. In certain institutions, hematologists may also oversee the management of hematology laboratories. Pathologists who specialize in diagnosing hematological diseases and primarily work in hematology laboratories are known as hematopathologists. Hematologists and hematopathologists often collaborate to establish accurate diagnoses and determine the most appropriate therapeutic interventions when necessary. Hematology is a distinct subspecialty of internal medicine, although it overlaps with the subspecialty of medical oncology. Hematologists may further specialize or develop specific interests in areas such as the treatment of bleeding disorders (e.g., hemophilia and idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura), hematological malignancies (e.g., lymphoma and leukemia, also known as onco-hematology), hemoglobinopathies, or the science of blood transfusion and blood bank operations. The term hematology is derived from the Greek word haima, meaning blood, and logos, meaning study or discourse. In clinical laboratories, the hematology department performs a wide range of blood tests. The most commonly conducted test is the complete blood count (CBC), also known as the full blood count (FBC). This test includes measurements such as white blood cell count, platelet count, hemoglobin levels, and various parameters related to red blood cells. Coagulation is a subspecialty within hematology. Basic coagulation tests include the prothrombin time (PT) and partial thromboplastin time (PTT). Another frequently performed hematology test is the erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), which measures the rate at which red blood cells settle in a test tube over a specified period. In blood banks, the Coombs test is one of the most commonly performed tests. This test is used to detect antibodies that may bind to red blood cells, which is critical in transfusion medicine.
